summary:
1. High-stayed hooks (>50% stayed) use active, direct statements that call out the viewer or drop a bold counter-intuitive fact immediately within 10 words, skipping all context.
2. Low-stayed hooks (<31% stayed) fail because they rely on slow story setups, hypothetical scenarios ('Your car swerves...'), or academic preambles before getting to the point.
3. Winning titles are short (<7 words) and frame the topic around common, personal bodily experiences or popular pop-culture icons (T. rex, leaking eyes, crying onions).
4. High AVP (>100%) requires high-information density in under 35 seconds, but stayed_pct determines initial reach, making sentence #1 the absolute bottleneck.
5. Avoid engineering specs or abstract space facts in titles; frame topics as direct questions or intriguing personal secrets.
winning_hooks: The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.
Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.
You are not sad when you chop an onion.
avoid: Pluto seemed like our solar system's edge, yet astronomers are investigating evidence that the Kuiper Belt extends much further than we once thought.
Your car swerves off the highway right toward a steel guardrail.
Fossilized bones can last millions of years, but sometimes they hide more than just minerals.
next_experiment: Test Hook Wording Directness: Take one topic (e.g., Guardrails) and release two versions with identical visuals but different opening lines—Arm A (Hypothetical setup): 'Imagine driving down the highway at 70 mph...'; Arm B (Direct callout statement): 'Guardrails don't block your car, they shred it.' Measure the stayed_pct gap.
